name: Pyruvic acid peel

lead: Pyruvic acid peels are superficial chemical peels applied in a clinic, mostly for acne. People book them to clear breakouts and refresh dull, congested skin.

Pyruvic acid is a keratolytic alpha-keto acid that loosens the outer skin layers so they shed, which clears pores and eases breakouts. Published work is small: a 2014 comparison of 50% pyruvic and 30% salicylic acid peels in 20 acne patients measured effects on facial sebum secretion.

paras: A clinician applies it in the office, and treatment is usually repeated as a series. Mild peeling follows, and sunscreen is used afterward.
Peels in general can cause redness, photosensitivity, pigment change and, rarely, scarring.

angle.text: People book pyruvic acid peels to clear active acne and refresh dull, congested skin. The keratolytic acid sheds the outer layer so pores clear and breakouts ease. A handful of small studies cover its use in acne.

lead: A pyruvic acid peel is a clinic-applied chemical peel that uses pyruvic acid, an alpha-keto acid, to loosen and shed the outer layers of skin. People have it done to reduce active acne, soften acne scars, even out pigmentation such as melasma, and improve skin texture, so skin looks clearer and smoother.[1][2][3][4][5]

Pyruvic acid is described as keratolytic, antimicrobial and sebostatic, and a 2006 study reports it can stimulate collagen and elastic fiber formation. Because it is small and has a low pKa it penetrates quickly, and a peel typically causes intense burning followed by redness, flaking and sometimes crusting.[4]

Pyruvic acid is also the simplest alpha-keto acid and a central molecule in cell metabolism, produced when glucose is broken down in glycolysis; as a peel ingredient it is applied topically in a clinic at concentrations that the studies cite at 25 to 70 percent.[1][2][6] It belongs to the family of chemical peels that has been used for skin resurfacing since the nineteenth century.[7]
Published evidence consists of small clinical studies, mostly 20 to 60 participants, covering acne, acne scars, melasma and photodamage.[1][2][3][4][5]
infobox: Sessions every 2 weeks for 8 to 12 weeks[2][3]

paras: Pyruvic acid is grouped with the superficial peeling agents, alongside alpha hydroxy acids such as glycolic acid and beta hydroxy acids such as salicylic acid.[5][7] Chemical peels as a class are used for fine lines, acne, acne scars and pigment changes. Wikipedia describes light peels as AHA and BHA peels done in offices or med spas, and medium-depth peels such as TCA as needing a medical provider.[7]
A 2022 study states pyruvic acid at 40 to 70 percent is used as a superficial to medium peeling agent.[2]

Pyruvic acid (CH3COCOOH) is the simplest alpha-keto acid, with a molar mass of about 88 g/mol and a pKa of 2.50, containing both a carboxylic acid and a ketone group.[6] Its low pKa and small size are cited as reasons it penetrates the skin quickly.[4][6] Berzelius named it in 1835 after obtaining it by heating tartaric acid, and its structure was settled by the 1870s.[6]

Chemical peeling as a practice dates to the Austrian dermatologist Ferdinand von Hebra in the second half of the nineteenth century, who used agents such as phenol and nitric acid to treat freckles and skin irregularities.[7] Peels are classified by depth and agent: alpha hydroxy acid peels such as glycolic and lactic acid are the mildest, beta hydroxy acid peels use salicylic acid, retinoic acid peels are deeper, and phenol-croton oil peels are the deepest.[7]

Wikipedia says light AHA and BHA peels usually need no anesthetic because patients feel only slight stinging, while medium-depth peels such as TCA cause more discomfort, with warmth or burning that may be eased with oral pain relievers or a tranquilizer.[7] A 2006 study describes pyruvic acid application as usually causing intense burning, followed by erythema, desquamation and sometimes crusting.[4]

In the melasma trial, patients were primed with 0.025 percent tretinoin cream daily for two weeks before peeling began, and peels were repeated every two weeks for 12 weeks.[3] Study protocols in acne used two-weekly peels over 12 weeks with follow-up at 24 weeks.[2]

Pyruvic acid application usually causes intense burning, and the post-peel period involves redness, desquamation and sometimes crusting.[4] Chemical peels of all strengths can cause photosensitivity, prolonged redness, pigmentary changes, milia, skin atrophy and scarring, according to Wikipedia.[7] Study exclusion criteria included a history of hypertrophic scarring, keloids and active or recurrent herpes.[2]
Pyruvic acid peels appear in looksmaxxing taxonomies as one of the clinic-based skin-resurfacing options in the hardmaxx category.

Acne: a 2014 study of 20 patients aged 13 to 30 compared a 50% pyruvic acid peel (10 patients) with a 30% salicylic acid peel (10 patients) and measured facial sebum secretion.[5] A 2022 study of 30 people with active acne, post-acne scarring and hyperpigmentation excluded those on oral antibiotics or topical acne medication in the previous four weeks, gave 40% pyruvic acid peels every two weeks for 12 weeks, followed patients to 24 weeks, and recorded a significant fall in comedones (p = 0.001) and papules.[2]

Acne scars: a 2023 randomized split-face trial of 30 patients with atrophic scars compared microneedling with 15% TCA against microneedling with 25% pyruvic acid. The mean ECCA scar score fell from about 151.2 to 138.8 on the TCA side and from about 151.8 to 141.3 on the pyruvic side at 21 weeks, with no significant difference between sides; patients and physicians rated moderate-to-marked improvement after three months, and the authors noted early reduction in rolling and boxcar scars compared with icepick scars.[1]

Melasma: a 2025 trial randomized 60 patients to 90% lactic acid or 40% pyruvic acid peels every two weeks for 12 weeks after tretinoin priming; MASI scores fell from 10.42 to 4.59 in the lactic group and from 9.65 to 4.53 in the pyruvic group, and quality of life was also assessed with MELASQoL.[3]

Photodamage: a 2006 study of 20 otherwise healthy subjects tested a new non-erythematogenic 50% pyruvic acid formulation (with dimethyl isosorbide, propylene glycol and other vehicles) in four sessions two weeks apart for photodamage, superficial scarring and melasma, monitoring changes with noninvasive instruments.[4]
